intro.label: Overview
intro.heading: What Is a Wirehaired Pointing Griffon?
intro.html:
The Wirehaired Pointing Griffon was developed in the late 19th century by Dutch breeder Eduard Karel Korthals with one explicit goal: create the most versatile hunting dog possible. The result is a medium-large sporting dog capable of pointing, flushing, and retrieving on all terrain and in water — earning the breed its reputation as the "supreme gun dog" or "4x4 of hunting dogs."

The wiry, harsh double coat provides protection from dense brush, cold water, and rough terrain. It's also low-shedding — a practical advantage for households. The coat has a distinctive unkempt, mustached appearance that makes the Griffon one of the more visually distinctive sporting breeds.

Off the hunting field, Wirehaired Pointing Griffons are affectionate, devoted, and good-natured family dogs. They bond closely with their family and want to be involved in household life. Their high energy requires management — a Griffon that hasn't had adequate exercise is a Griffon that will find its own stimulation.

appearance.label: Physical
appearance.heading: What Wirehaired Pointing Griffons Look Like
appearance.html:
Medium to large build — 35–70 lbs with a significant size variation, 20–24 inches at the shoulder. The body is strong and athletic, built for endurance rather than pure speed. The face is framed by a distinctive bushy mustache and eyebrows that are characteristic of the breed.

The double coat consists of a harsh, wiry outer coat and a thick undercoat. Steel gray with brown markings is the classic color, though variations including chestnut, roan, and white-and-brown occur. The coat does not shed heavily and is considered low-shedding compared to most sporting breeds, but it does require maintenance to prevent matting and maintain the protective wiry texture.

temperament.label: Personality
temperament.heading: Temperament
temperament.html:
Wirehaired Pointing Griffons are loyal, affectionate, and strongly bonded to their family. They are typically good with children and generally get along well with other dogs when socialized. With strangers, most are friendly or at least neutral — less reserved than some sporting breeds, more approachable than guard breeds.

The energy level in a working context is very high — these are dogs built for full days in the field. At home with adequate exercise, they settle well. Without adequate exercise, they're restless, vocal, and potentially destructive. This is not a breed for sedentary households.

Intelligence is high. They learn quickly and genuinely want to work with their handler. Training is rewarding with this breed — they pick up field commands, obedience work, and dog sports readily. Their working instincts can occasionally override their manners around birds or small game, so reliable recall requires real training investment.

mikes_take.label: A Realistic Take
mikes_take.heading: What I'd Tell a Friend Thinking About a Wirehaired Pointing Griffon
mikes_take.html:
For hunting households, the Wirehaired Pointing Griffon is hard to beat. Versatile, intelligent, low-shedding, and with a personality that makes them excellent home companions in addition to superb hunters. The breed is increasingly popular and quality breeders are more accessible than the rarer sporting breeds.

For non-hunting households, the Griffon works well provided they get genuine daily exercise. Dog sports — hunt tests, agility, tracking, scent work — give the working drive an outlet. A Griffon with an active owner who runs, hikes, or participates in dog sports will be a fantastic companion.

The coat is practical — low-shedding and weather-resistant — but it needs maintenance. Hand-stripping preserves the working texture for hunting dogs; regular trimming is fine for companion dogs. Either way, the ears need weekly attention to prevent infections.

care.label: Daily Life
care.heading: Care Requirements
care.html:
Exercise

High energy — 90+ minutes of vigorous exercise daily. Off-leash running in safe areas, field work, hunting, agility, and hiking are all suitable. This breed needs to run, not just walk. A leash walk is insufficient for daily exercise needs.

Grooming

The wiry coat is low-maintenance relative to feathered spaniels, but it's not no-maintenance. Brushing 1–2 times per week. For working dogs, hand-stripping 1–2 times per year preserves the harsh wiry texture that protects in the field. For companion dogs, regular trimming is acceptable. Weekly ear cleaning is essential. See the Wirehaired Pointing Griffon grooming guide for details.

Training

Easy to moderately easy — intelligent, willing, and handler-focused. Positive reinforcement works well. Field training is natural for this breed; basic obedience should begin early and be maintained. Recall requires consistent training given strong prey drive.

health.label: Wellness
health.heading: Health & Common Conditions
health.html:
Wirehaired Pointing Griffons are generally healthy with a 12–15 year lifespan. The primary health concerns are hip dysplasia, thyroid disease, eye issues, and ear infections.

ConditionWhat It Means
Hip DysplasiaMalformed hip joint causing pain and arthritis. OFA or PennHIP screening available. Ask breeders for clearances on both parents.
HypothyroidismUnderactive thyroid — manageable with daily medication. OFA thyroid clearance available from breeders.
Eye IssuesHereditary eye conditions occur in the breed. CAER eye exam clearance from breeders is important.
Ear InfectionsThe drop ears trap moisture and debris, particularly in dogs working in water. Weekly ear cleaning and keeping ear canal hair trimmed is essential prevention.

Ask breeders for: OFA hip, OFA thyroid, CAER eye exam clearances.

Active non-hunting owners who run, hike, or participate in dog sports
Households who want a low-shedding sporting breed
Families who want an affectionate, loyal companion alongside a working dog
Owners committed to providing significant daily exercise
not_fit: You work full-time with 8+ hours away from home — Wirehaired Pointing Griffons need 90+ min of vigorous daily activity, and under-exercised dogs of this breed often develop destructive chewing, barking, or separation anxiety
You have a small apartment without nearby outdoor space — at 35–70 lbs, Wirehaired Pointing Griffons need room to stretch and a routine of off-property exercise
Sedentary households — this breed needs real work or vigorous exercise
Owners who want a breed that's immediately satisfied with leash walks
Those who want minimal grooming — ear and coat maintenance is required

finding.label: Next Steps
finding.heading: Finding Your Wirehaired Pointing Griffon
finding.html:
Buying from a Breeder

$1,500–$3,000 from reputable breeders. Required health clearances: OFA hip, OFA thyroid, CAER eye. The American Wirehaired Pointing Griffon Association maintains a breeder referral directory. Many breeders also do NAVHDA testing on their breeding dogs — look for titled dogs in working-dog pedigrees.

Rescue

Wirehaired Pointing Griffon rescue exists through the American Wirehaired Pointing Griffon Association. Available dogs are typically adults with known histories.

Before your Griffon comes home, review the Wirehaired Pointing Griffon puppy checklist — exercise setup and early field introduction planning are the first priorities.

faq.q: What makes the Wirehaired Pointing Griffon a versatile gun dog?
faq.a: The breed was specifically developed to point upland game, flush it when commanded, and retrieve both on land and from water — covering all three major roles of a gun dog in one animal. The harsh coat provides protection from dense brush, cold water, and rough terrain. Most sporting breeds specialize; the Griffon was bred to do everything.

Minimally. The harsh wiry double coat sheds significantly less than most sporting breeds. This makes them one of the better choices for households wanting a sporting dog without heavy shedding. The coat does require regular brushing and either hand-stripping (for working dogs) or professional trimming to maintain.

faq.q: Are Wirehaired Pointing Griffons good family dogs?
faq.a: Yes — when adequately exercised. They're affectionate, loyal, and good with children. The key variable is exercise: a Griffon with 90+ minutes of vigorous daily activity is a calm, pleasant house dog. An under-exercised Griffon is restless and difficult.

faq.q: What is hand-stripping and do I need to do it?
faq.a: Hand-stripping is a grooming technique that removes dead outer coat by pulling it out rather than cutting it, which preserves the harsh wiry texture of the working coat. For hunting dogs, hand-stripping maintains the protective coat quality. For companion dogs, regular trimming with scissors or clippers is acceptable and easier, though it softens the coat texture over time.
